source.title: Steering Language Model Refusal with Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Kyle O'Brien; D. Majercak; Xavier Fernandes; Richard Edgar; Jingya Chen; Harsha Nori; Dean Carignan; Eric Horvitz; F. Poursabzi-Sangdeh

page_placements.theme: Reconstruction substitution can preserve task performance

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses SAE reconstructions and a reconstruction-error term in its feature-steering setup, but does not investigate the structure or scaling of SAE errors.
record.gate_note: Table 10 reports benchmark scores with SAE reconstruction and no steering. It does not compare SAE errors with random errors, test linear predictability, or sweep SAE size. Other refusal-steering results do not measure the claim's versions.
record.test_reason: The paper is about refusal steering with a Top-k SAE on Phi-3 Mini and Llama 3.1 8B. It adds the SAE error term back during steering (Section 3.1; Appendix A.1) but never studies the error itself. There is no linear prediction of the error, no sweep of SAE size, no random-error control, no with- versus without-error comparison, and no training ablation. Its only reconstruction result (Table 10) is a sanity check of benchmark scores.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that amplifying SAE refusal features improves robustness to single-turn and multi-turn jailbreaks. They find this comes with over-refusal and broad benchmark degradation, which also appears when steering a philosophy feature and in Llama. They take this to suggest the features are entangled with general capabilities, and that conditional steering reduces the tradeoff. They draw no conclusions about SAE error or dark matter.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains Top-k SAEs and clamps refusal-related features for test-time steering; it does not analyze reconstruction-error predictability, scaling, or structure.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that steering outcomes vary with clamp value and, in its Llama experiments, with the selected feature. These settings concern steering effects, not SAE error structure.

fits_no_version.finding: With SAE reconstruction and no steering, Phi-3 Mini scores 66.46% on MMLU, 66.25% on TruthfulQA and 85.67% on GSM8k, against 68.80%, 65.00% and 82.50% for the original model. The authors call this largely unaffected.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For this layer-6 Top-k SAE, SAE reconstruction without steering leaves benchmark scores near the original model's.

record.problems: The results relevant to SAE reconstruction are benchmark scores only; there is no random-error comparison, direct loss measure, or analysis of error vectors.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported results were left out. Refusal, jailbreak, and feature-steering outcomes do not measure the specified dark-matter claims.

untested.parts: All: no linear regression of the SAE error on input activations.
All: a single SAE size (expansion factor 8, k=32), with no per-token error-norm analysis.
All: no comparison of loss under SAE reconstruction with loss under random errors of the same size.
All: no split of the error into linear and nonlinear parts.
All: steering keeps the error term, but no comparison with versus without it is reported.
All: no architecture or objective ablation. Figure 10 gives FVU and dead-latent percentages by layer only, not as tests of dark matter.

record.verdict_notes: Appendix A.1 says the error term l = x - x̂ is optionally added to the steered reconstruction, and Section 3.1 says it was used. Table 10 does not state whether l was included. If it was, the score differences would reflect evaluation noise, not reconstruction error. This ambiguity is why r1–r3 cannot inform V3 or V5. The study cites Engels et al. (the original source) but does not test it.

versions.untested_parts: Linear predictability of SAE error from input activations and the share of error so predictable.
Per-token error-norm predictability across SAE sizes, overlap of failed contexts across sizes, and whether error persists with scale.
No comparison of model loss after SAE reconstruction against random errors of the same size.
The study does not distinguish linearly predictable and nonlinear error components or test their relation to learned features and further dictionary learning.
No comparison tests whether SAE-based analyses or interventions preserve model behavior with versus without the error term.
No ablation of sparsity penalty, shrinkage, dead latents, objective, architecture, or end-to-end training as explanations for dark matter.

rows.subject: Phi-3 Mini
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate benchmark performance using SAE reconstruction with no steering.
rows.note: The paper says benchmark performance is largely unaffected by SAE reconstruction; this result does not compare error against a random-error control.
rows.check: This is a sanity check of the SAE setup, not a test of any version. It has no random-error control (V3), and it is not stated whether the error term was added back in Table 10 (V5). Section 3.1 says reconstruction and error are combined, which would reproduce the original activations exactly. Yet the scores differ from the baseline. So the condition cannot be read.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: Section 3.1 combines the steered reconstruction with the error term, but no experiment isolates the error's contribution or tests any claim version.

tranche.reason: The study retains the reconstruction error during feature steering and evaluates steering performance, without testing error predictability, scaling, pathology, decomposition, functional necessity, or training artifacts.

source_check.notes: Table 10 confirms all three benchmark comparisons but does not specify whether the error term was retained. Section 3.1 retains it during steering; Appendix A.1 describes retention as optional. The supplied text is arXiv v2, dated 22 May 2025.
